summary: This document extends the basic IP fast reroute mechanism in RFC 5286 to give extra backup connectivity for point-to-point link failures when the basic mechanisms cannot offer any.

eli5.summary: If a road is closed and there is no simple detour, this finds a path through a tunnel that still gets you there.

questions: ip fast reroute remote loop-free alternate
how does ip fast reroute work
subtitle: When no neighbor can safely catch your traffic after a link fails, tunnel it to a router that can.

tldr.problem: Basic Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs) need a direct neighbor that can deliver traffic without sending it back over the failed link. Some topologies, notably rings, have no such neighbor.
tldr.mechanism: The router that detects the failure pre-builds a tunnel to a remote 'PQ node' that is reachable without using the failed link and from which normal forwarding will not come back over it. Repair traffic is sent through that tunnel.
tldr.outcome: In the RFC's study of 14 real service provider topologies, remote LFA gave close to 100% protection against link failure in 11 of them. It covers point-to-point link failures only, not node failures.

facts.label: Default PQ choice
facts.value: Lowest cost from S, ties to lowest node identifier

today: RFC 7490 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It builds on the basic LFA mechanism of RFC 5286.

sections.title: Why Plain LFAs Fall Short
sections.content:
IP Fast Reroute lets a router switch to a precomputed backup path the moment an adjacent link fails, instead of waiting for the network to reconverge. The basic mechanism, Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs) from RFC 5286, works well in highly meshed networks, as RFC 6571 discusses.

It struggles in some topologies, notably rings. The reason is that no neighbor of the Point of Local Repair (PLR), the router next to the failure, has a path to the destination that avoids the failure and is also cheaper than the path through the failure.

RFC 7490 extends the LFA idea by tunneling the packets that need repair to a node that the PLR can reach and that can reach the destination.
sections.eli5: Normally a router has a neighbor it can hand traffic to when a link breaks. In a ring there may be no neighbor that can help, so this RFC finds help further away.

sections.title: P-space, Q-space and PQ Nodes
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few sets of routers with respect to a protected link S-E, where S is the repairing router and E is the router at the far end of the link.

  • P-space of S: routers S can reach on its pre-convergence shortest paths without any of those paths (including equal-cost splits) crossing S-E.
  • Extended P-space: the union of the P-spaces of S's neighbors (leaving out the one reached over the protected link). S can pick which neighbor it forces the repair packet to, so it may use these larger sets.
  • Q-space of E: routers that can reach E without any path crossing S-E.
  • PQ node: a node in both the (extended) P-space of S and the Q-space of E. The repair tunnel endpoint is chosen from the PQ nodes.

A repair tunnel is a tunnel set up to give S a virtual neighbor that is a Loop-Free Alternate, and remote LFA (RLFA) means using a PQ node rather than a direct neighbor as the next hop of an LFA repair.
sections.eli5: P-space is everywhere you can get to without using the broken road. Q-space is everywhere that can get to the far side of the broken road without using it. The best tunnel exit is a place that is in both.

sections.title: The Ring Example and the Tunnel Idea
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC is a ring of six routers: S, E, D, C, B and A. With equal link costs, traffic crossing S-E cannot be fully protected by LFAs. The destination C is an equal-cost multipath from S, so it is protectable, but traffic to D and E is not.

S can reach A, B and C without using S-E, so those form its extended P-space. D and C can reach E without S-E, so they form E's Q-space. B is excluded because it has equal-cost paths to E, one of which goes through S-E. The only node in both sets is C, so C becomes the tunnel endpoint. Once a tunnel S to C exists, C acts as a direct neighbor of S and is an LFA for D and E.

The tunnel carries only repair traffic and MUST NOT be used for normal traffic, so non-failure traffic distribution is unchanged. OAM traffic that verifies the repair path MAY use the tunnel before a failure.
sections.eli5: In a ring, S finds one far-away router, C, that it can reach the long way round and that can reach the other side of the break. S builds a tunnel to C and uses it only when the road breaks.

sections.title: Repair Tunnels and How They Are Built
sections.content:
Repair paths are precomputed so they can be activated as soon as a failure is detected. A repair tunnel MUST be provisioned beforehand, and since its location is worked out dynamically it has to be set up automatically. Several repair tunnels may share an endpoint. The tunnel MUST NOT traverse the link S-E, and it ends at an intermediate router, not at E itself.

The endpoint must satisfy two properties: it MUST be reachable from the tunnel source without crossing the failed link, and packets released from the tunnel MUST proceed to their destination without being attracted back over the failed link.

Computing the set takes three steps: find the P-space (a shortest path tree from S with the subtree through S-E removed), widen it to the extended P-space using trees rooted at S's neighbors, and find the Q-space with a reverse shortest path tree rooted at E. The Q-space of E is used as a proxy for each destination's Q-space, because a per-destination calculation would need an SPF run per destination, which is not considered scalable.

If several PQ nodes qualify, it is RECOMMENDED that the one with the lowest cost from S be the default, with ties going to the lowest node identifier (SHOULD). Choosing the closest maximizes load balancing after release from the tunnel. The RFC also gives a cost-based pseudocode algorithm. Whether to prefer an ordinary LFA over a remote one is a local matter.
sections.eli5: The router works out the backup tunnel ahead of time, so when a road breaks it can switch at once. If there are several possible exits it usually picks the nearest one.

sections.title: Tunnels in Practice and LDP
sections.content:
The choice of tunneling mechanism is outside the scope of the RFC. It names IP-in-IP (RFC 1853) and GRE (RFC 1701) as options. In an MPLS network using LDP (RFC 5036), a simple label stack (RFC 3032) does the job, with no new protocol extension: the outer label is S's neighbor's label for the tunnel endpoint, and the inner label is the endpoint's label for the packet destination.

To learn that inner label, S needs a targeted LDP session with the endpoint. No protection exists until that session is up and the label is learned, and if it cannot be established an implementation SHOULD tell the operator through network management. Ideally the endpoint advertises its targeted LDP address in the IGP; without such a protocol, an LSR should try the Router ID unless configured otherwise.

The RFC also says to take IS-IS overload, OSPF stub router advertisement (RFC 6987) and costed-out links into account. The PLR MUST NOT use a tunnel endpoint with the IS-IS overload bit set, or one where all outgoing interfaces have the cost set to MaxLinkMetric for OSPF.
sections.eli5: In networks that already use labels like tickets, the tunnel is just one extra ticket on top of the packet. The router first has to phone the exit router to ask which ticket to use.

sections.title: Node Failures, Examples and Real-World Results
sections.content:
The technique targets point-to-point link failures. It does not cover a failed broadcast or NBMA interface. For node failures or shared risk link group failures there is a danger that repairs loop, because two neighbors of the failed node may each try to repair via the other. The RFC lists ways to reduce this: drop a packet that arrives on the interface used to reach the first hop of the RLFA path, require the repair target's path to the destination never to pass through E, or require that another neighbor on the path be downstream. It also says an operator may judge node failure rare enough to ignore.

In the RFC's service provider example (Figure 3), PE1 and PE2 sit in one site with a low metric of 5 between them, and metric 1000 on the P-PE links. Raising the PE1-PE2 metric to allow an LFA would risk higher latency, but remote LFA gives full protection with PE1 choosing P2 and PE2 choosing P1.

The RFC analyzed 14 real service provider topologies collected between the end of 2012 and early 2013. Remote LFA provided close to 100% prefix protection against link failure in 11 of the 14 and a significant improvement in two of the remaining three. For example, topology 1 went from 78.5% protected with LFA alone to 99.7% with RLFA. The gain in guaranteed node protection was normally modest.
sections.eli5: The tunnel trick is good for a single broken road. If a whole junction goes down, two helpers might send cars back and forth to each other, so the RFC lists ways to avoid that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5286 also apply. Targeted LDP sessions and MPLS tunnels are normal features of an MPLS network, and the RFC says their use here raises no additional security concerns.

IP repair tunnel endpoints, where used, SHOULD be assigned from addresses that are not reachable from outside the routing domain, so they cannot be used as an attack vector. Apart from OAM traffic, only traffic protected because of a link failure goes into the tunnel, and the repair tunnel MUST NOT be advertised by the routing protocol as a link that may carry normal user traffic or routing protocol traffic.
sections.eli5: The secret tunnel should be hidden from outsiders and used only for emergencies, never as a regular road.

items.title: P-space
items.text: Routers S reaches without crossing the protected link S-E.

items.text: The union of the P-spaces of S's other neighbors.
